39519-agincourt-a-romance-the-works-of-g:
Agincourt, a Romance forms volume twenty of the collected works of G P R James. The set was revised and corrected by James himself. A long French preface argues for the worth of the romance as a form. It praises tales that teach by example and scorns those that wallow in vice.

The title names the great English win in France in fourteen fifteen. James built his name on tales set in past ages, with kings, knights, and wars at their core. A romance on Agincourt would mix the famed battle with love, honour, and court life. The volume suits readers who like old-style tales of chivalry told at full length.
41645-the-milkmaid-of-montfermeil-novels:
Paul de Kock, the French novelist, wrote this tale, and this entry holds volume twenty of his novels in English dress, printed at Boston and New York. The front picture shows Denise, the little milkmaid of Montfermeil, led to the altar by the man she loves, while the whole village watches. The story opens in a cabriolet, where a friend tells a lieutenant he cannot go on as he has.

The talk turns to Caesar dictating four letters at once and to Pico de la Mirandola, who claimed to know everything. Such banter sets the book's comic, worldly tone. De Kock was famous for lively tales of Paris life and love. This volume follows a village girl whose wedding crowns the story.
58043-the-century-illustrated-monthly-ma:
The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine for August nineteen thirteen is volume eighty-six, number four, billed as the midsummer holiday number. The Century Company held the rights for nineteen thirteen. A contents list, drawn from the May index, opens the hosted text.

The lead tale, The White Linen Nurse by Eleanor Hallowell Abbott, starts on page four hundred and eighty-three. Herman Pfeifer drew its pictures, printed in tint. Alvan F Sanborn writes on Romain Rolland, with a portrait after Granié. Robert Hichens skirts the Balkan Peninsula, reaching Stamboul, the city of mosques. Jules Guérin made the pictures, two in colour.
65289-munchausen-xx:
Munchausen Twenty is a tall tale book by a self styled Baron, published at Chicago in 1904. Its title page promises wondrous but veracious happenings which befell his ancestors in the text. They are translated and first printed from manuscripts found most miraculously by himself in that account. Curtis drew the illustrations that bring the episodes nearer to the reader.

The book contains, as well, his adventures in securing those remarkable documents for the world. A very entrancing series of thrilling incidents of his own life is set forth in the title. They took place prior to and while searching for the glorious creature whose husband he becomes in the tale. The volume is an American Munchausen, a liar romance of 1904 in which the Baron line is renewed on the far side of the Atlantic with a straight face.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xix:
Pope John XIX, enthroned in 1024, dead in 1032, shares one entry with John XX. A listed pope who never lived scrambled the Johns' numbering. When the last Crescentius patricius died, Tusculum's counts grabbed Rome's reins. One of their line climbed as Benedict VIII, while his brother Romanus wielded temporal power as consul and senator.

After Benedict died, Romanus, still a layman, won election between 12 April and 10 May 1024. He took every order in turn, assumed John's name, and courted Romans with lavish spending. Soon the Byzantine Emperor Basil II sent envoys begging the pope to acknowledge the oecumenical patriarch's title, bearing rich gifts to sway him. The talks stayed secret at first, but once the matter surfaced, public feeling forced John to turn down the Byzantine bids and gifts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xxi:
Pope John XXI, Lisbon-born between 1210 and 1220, took the throne in 1276 and died at Viterbo 20 May 1277. Julianus fathered him; baptised Peter, he went by Petrus Juliani or Petrus Hispanus. Lisbon's cathedral school gave him his first lessons, then Paris University, where he heard dialectics, logic, and above all Aristotelian physics and metaphysics from Albertus Magnus.

Natural philosophy drew Peter most. He took up medicine and theology, joining the Minorite master John of Parma. Once his studies ended, Siena's university, then fast growing, called him in 1247 to teach medicine. There he composed his Summulae logicales, logic's favourite textbook for almost three hundred years. The book tracks the Paris method and William Shyreswood's compendium, Shyreswood being Peter's teacher there. At Siena he also gathered a sheaf of medical prescriptions.
